II. Abstrakt
Handel, so wie viele andere Aspekte der Wirtschaft, hat die Förderung des Wohlstands zum
Ziel. Die Entwicklung des Handels, wenn sie zielorientiert geführt ist, stellt eine Gelegenheit
für wirtschaftliches Wachstum dar, schafft Arbeitsplätze und Reichtum und mindert die
Armut. Da der Handel auch die Bürger betrifft, wendet jedes Land seine eigene
Handelspolitik in Erfüllung der Bedürfnisse und Verlangen seiner Bürger an. Die
Europäische Union und die Vereinigten Staaten sind die weltgrössten Handelsmächte. Dies
erklärt auch, warum ihre Handelspolitiken eine gewaltige Rolle in der Entwicklung des
Welthandelsverkehr sowie in der weltweiten Förderung der Sozialhilfen, spielen.
Über die letzten Jahrzehnte hinweg haben die Europäische Union, die Vereinigten Staaten
und einige andere Länder Verhandlungen bezüglich der Abschaffung von Handelsbarrieren
begonnen. Diese haben dazu geführt, dass die Bedeutung des Handels und vor allem die des
internationalen Handels drastisch gestiegen ist.
Die Erweiterung des Anwendungsbereiches der Handelspolitiken ist notwendig um in den
verschiedensten Märkten der Welt Wettbewerb zu erzielen. Liberalisierte Handelsordnungen
spielen daher eine bedeutende Rolle in der Entwicklung wettbewerbsfähiger Handelsmärkte.
Auf internationalem Niveau gibt es zurzeit eine gemeinsame Vorgehensweise bezüglich der
Nutzung von 'Handelsrechtsmittel' um den Handel zu schützen und unterstützen. Heutzutage

## dimension
As showed in the previous chapter, WTO law provides the multilateral framework of
international trade relationships between states. The Organisation has 157 Members
out of 198 countries in the world and aspires to universal cover age. Since all major
global players and the large majority of developing countries are WTO Members, the
organisation is the accepted point of reference for international trade regulation.
Beside the WTO, there are around 200 bilateral and plurilateral trad e agreements
concluded between WTO Members that make the legislation more complex and the
bigger picture more difficult to obtain. These agreements remain outside the WTO
institutional framework and provide regulation on import and export of food that can
go considerably beyond existing multilateral trade law in terms of elimination of trade
barriers. Bilateral and plurilateral trade agreements supplement multilateral trade law
in the relationship between the parties but create no obligations for other coun tries.
The EU has a plethora of ways to intervene in this complex body of norms and
use them extensively. The Directorate General for External Trade of the European
Commission, one of the largest, put in place a broad policy to participate in the
evolutio n of international trade law and promotes its modification alongside precise
policy objectives defined by EU institutions. These policies are designed completely
at EU level because the Treaty of Lisbon gives EU institutions exclusive competence
on externa l trade. Accordingly, the EU Commission represents Member States during
WTO negotiations and negotiates free trade agreements with partner countries. This
section introduces four aspects of the EU external trade policy. First, we present the
legal basis fo r the EU external action with regard to international trade law. Second,
we explain the procedures and the institutions involved in the design and conclusion 70
of international trade agreements. Third, we provide a brief reflection on the role of
member stat es during trade negotiations. Finally, the section summarises the ways
with which the EU intervenes on international trade law within the WTO framework
and outside of it (through free trade agreements).

## (a) Competence
Since the Treaty of Rome the internat ional commerce of goods between Members of
the European Economic Community (EC) and third states has been a core competence
of its institutions . To this crucial but limited prerogative the EC and the EU added
additional external powers through treaty amend ments and the case law of the
European Court of Justice. The treaty of Lisbon represents today the point of arrival
of more than 50 years of evolution of EU competences in the realm of external trade
and provides the EU with an extensive and exclusive grou nd to act with regard to
international trade regulation. 132 Notably, the Treaty of Lisbon extended the EU
exclusive competence much beyond the international trade of goods fully including
international trade in services and trade -related issues such as intel lectual property
and investment. 133 In particular, the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
includes a general part on EU external relations that provides a list of objectives that
the EU should pursue in its relationship with third countries and through its action in
international organisations. Article 21 provides several objectives closely linked with
the EU international commercial policy. Paragraph (e) of Article 21 provides that the
EU shall “encourage the integration of all countries into th e world economy including
progressive abolition of restrictions on international trade” and paragraph (d) requires
that the EU “foster[s] the sustainable economic, social and environmental
development of developing countries with the primary aim of eradica ting poverty”. 134

As we shall see below, the EU external commercial policy is much more than

The conclusion of trade agreements with third countries and the participation to the

## 2. Summary of the main findi ngs of the first four chapters

through this article the EU is enabled to conclude free trade agreements with countrie s
vulnerable to food shortages and w hen concluding a trade deal of this sort WTO law
oblige s to eliminate the large majority of import barriers. This has to be done even
when the agreement is concluded between developed countries and countries

of the right to food it has to move it two directions. On the one hand it has to work in
the Doha Round towards the modification of WTO law whenever the existing

## 3. Main findings of the case studies
The thesis included the case study of seven free trade agreements between the EU a nd
countries vulnerable to food shortages. Chapter 6 analysed from the perspective of the
human right to food the trade agreement between the EU and 15 Caribbean countries ,
one of the most comprehensive trade agreements the EU has concluded so far.
Chapter 7 took into account a group of six interim trade agreements between the EU
and countries in Sub -Saharan Africa. From the case studies emerged that all the
clauses on import and export of food (tariffs, safeguards and export restrictions)
reduce the capaci ty of the developing countries involved to react to food shortages.
First, all the agreements in order to respect the prescriptions of Article XXIV GATT
eliminate at least 80% of tariff protection exposing vulnerable countries to increasing
competition fro m the EU and limiting their capacity to intervene at the occurrence of
import surges of food from the EU. The Food and Agriculture Organisation considers
import surges dangerous for the realisation of the right to food because they disrupt
the livelihood o f vulnerable farmers already exposed to hunger. To avoid this issue all
the treaties exclude certain sensitive products from the obligation of eliminating
import tariffs. Notwithstanding these exceptions the large majority of EU food
products will be impor ted in the Caribbean and African countries duty free. The
African agreements include additional limitations on the maximum tariff applicable to
sensitive food products imported from the EU . The new regulation promotes EU food
exports in vulnerable countrie s even when this exposes vulnerable groups to food
insecurity. In other words the policy support s the EU export business even if
increasing imports of food in the developing country affect the realisation of the right
to food. The treaties are also likely to affect public revenues of developing countries
hampering their capacity to organise policies to realise the right to food. Overall , the
analysis of the clauses on tariffs manifested the necessity of revising Article XXIV
GATT to allow differential treat ment when vulnerable countries are involved trade
agreements with the EU. Certain aspects of the regulation of tariffs however show that
the negotiators also pursued the objective of imposing limits on developing countries
beyond what required by WTO law. For instance, this is the case of the inclusion of a
maximum tariff for sensitive products imported in African countries which is much
lower than what is required by WTO law.

## 3. Main findings of the case studies
Second, the assessment of the clauses on import safeguards showed that
during ne gotiations very little effort was made to provide Caribbean and African
countries with an efficient mechanism of protection at the occurrence of import surges
of food from the EU. In particular, the treaties do not include a special safeguard
system like t he one of the WTO Agreement on Agriculture which would have allowed
automatic protection of domestic markets in adverse market conditions. The
safeguards provided are slow to implement, are supervised by a supranational
authority and contain almost no diff erential treatment between the EU and vulnerable
countries. In addition, in the African agreements there is no reference to the
possibility of using safeguards to protect food security. The safeguards contained in
the Caribbean agreement contain a referenc e to food security which, even if important
in terms of interpretation of the treaty, looks rhetorical since it does not make the
safeguards easier to implement. The similarities between the regulation of safeguards
of all the seven treaties taken into acc ount manifest that little efforts were made to
tailor the food safeguards on the specific necessities of each vulnerable country. 188
Finally, the regulation of export restrictions of all the agreements limit s
considerably the capacity of developing countries to use them to intervene on the
quantity of food exported abroad at the occurrence of food shortages . This is
particularly evident in the Caribbean case and in four of the African treaties which
ban export quotas and most of export taxes. It is particular ly regrettable that in these
five treaties the negotiators decided not to reproduce the exception of Article XI.2(a)
GATT that in the WTO system allows the use of export quotas to relieve food
shortages. Two of the African agreements maintained the excepti on even if they
include a regulation of export taxes considerably more restrictive of WTO. Moreover,
the prohibition of export taxes is likely to affect public revenues especially in the
African countries which are scarcely industrialised but rich in natur al resources. This
decision deprives vulnerable countries of an additional source of revenues even if the
clauses on tariffs already have an impact on public funding. The deficiencies of the
regulation of exports is particularly relevant for the examination of the EU external

In conclusion, all the seven treaties taken into account in this thesis diminish

II. Abstrakt
Handel, so wie viele andere Aspekte der Wirtschaft, hat die Förderung des Wohlstands zum
Ziel. Die Entwicklung des Handels, wenn sie zielorientiert geführt ist, stellt eine Gelegenheit
für wirtschaftliches Wachstum dar, schafft Arbeitsplätze und Reichtum und mindert die
Armut. Da der Handel auch die Bürger betrifft, wendet jedes Land seine eigene
Handelspolitik in Erfüllung der Bedürfnisse und Verlangen seiner Bürger an. Die
Europäische Union und die Vereinigten Staaten sind die weltgrössten Handelsmächte. Dies
erklärt auch, warum ihre Handelspolitiken eine gewaltige Rolle in der Entwicklung des
Welthandelsverkehr sowie in der weltweiten Förderung der Sozialhilfen, spielen.
Über die letzten Jahrzehnte hinweg haben die Europäische Union, die Vereinigten Staaten
und einige andere Länder Verhandlungen bezüglich der Abschaffung von Handelsbarrieren
begonnen. Diese haben dazu geführt, dass die Bedeutung des Handels und vor allem die des
internationalen Handels drastisch gestiegen ist.
Die Erweiterung des Anwendungsbereiches der Handelspolitiken ist notwendig um in den
verschiedensten Märkten der Welt Wettbewerb zu erzielen. Liberalisierte Handelsordnungen
spielen daher eine bedeutende Rolle in der Entwicklung wettbewerbsfähiger Handelsmärkte.
Auf internationalem Niveau gibt es zurzeit eine gemeinsame Vorgehensweise bezüglich der
Nutzung von 'Handelsrechtsmittel' um den Handel zu schützen und unterstützen. Heutzutage

Berücksichtigt man die oben erläuterten Informationen, dann war der Hauptgrund das Thema
- ‘Handelsverordnungen: eine vergleichende Analyse der Vorgehensweisen in den
Vereinigten Staaten und Europa – zu wählen, um einen tieferen Einblick und eine kurze
Analyse der Verordnungen dieser beiden riesigen Handelsmächte zu bekommen. Was sind
die Gemeinsamkeiten oder Differenzen in diesen zwei grossen Systemen? Das Interesse
daran, in den Gesetzgebungen dieser zwei Länder zu forschen lässt sich von ihrer Bedeutung 8
im Welthandel ableiten.
Handel spielt eine wahnsinnig grosse Rolle in der Entwicklung des Weltmarkts und die
grösste Arbeit ist es, den Markt in einer Art und Weise zu regulieren, dass man soviel wie
möglich aus der Entwicklung des Welthandels ziehen kann. Diese Handelsverordnungen sind
notwendig um mit wirtschaftlichen Hindernissen bezüglich des Marktzugangs und Import-
Export bezogenen Schwierigkeiten, welche eventuell ein Resultat von
Regierungsinterventionen und weltweiten Marktverordnungen sind, umzugehen.
Ich würde mich gerne mit diesem Thema beschäftigen um herauszufinden, welches die
Grundprinzipien und aktuellen Handelsverordnungen sind, und was ihr Einfluss auf den
Weltmarkt von heute ist. In meiner Thesis werde ich die Vorgehensweise der Vereinigten

## dimension
As showed in the previous chapter, WTO law provides the multilateral framework of
international trade relationships between states. The Organisation has 157 Members
out of 198 countries in the world and aspires to universal cover age. Since all major
global players and the large majority of developing countries are WTO Members, the
organisation is the accepted point of reference for international trade regulation.
Beside the WTO, there are around 200 bilateral and plurilateral trad e agreements
concluded between WTO Members that make the legislation more complex and the
bigger picture more difficult to obtain. These agreements remain outside the WTO
institutional framework and provide regulation on import and export of food that can
go considerably beyond existing multilateral trade law in terms of elimination of trade
barriers. Bilateral and plurilateral trade agreements supplement multilateral trade law
in the relationship between the parties but create no obligations for other coun tries.
The EU has a plethora of ways to intervene in this complex body of norms and
use them extensively. The Directorate General for External Trade of the European
Commission, one of the largest, put in place a broad policy to participate in the
evolutio n of international trade law and promotes its modification alongside precise
policy objectives defined by EU institutions. These policies are designed completely
at EU level because the Treaty of Lisbon gives EU institutions exclusive competence
on externa l trade. Accordingly, the EU Commission represents Member States during
WTO negotiations and negotiates free trade agreements with partner countries. This
section introduces four aspects of the EU external trade policy. First, we present the
legal basis fo r the EU external action with regard to international trade law. Second,
we explain the procedures and the institutions involved in the design and conclusion 70
of international trade agreements. Third, we provide a brief reflection on the role of
member stat es during trade negotiations. Finally, the section summarises the ways
with which the EU intervenes on international trade law within the WTO framework
and outside of it (through free trade agreements).

## (a) Competence
Since the Treaty of Rome the internat ional commerce of goods between Members of
the European Economic Community (EC) and third states has been a core competence
of its institutions . To this crucial but limited prerogative the EC and the EU added
additional external powers through treaty amend ments and the case law of the
European Court of Justice. The treaty of Lisbon represents today the point of arrival
of more than 50 years of evolution of EU competences in the realm of external trade
and provides the EU with an extensive and exclusive grou nd to act with regard to
international trade regulation. 132 Notably, the Treaty of Lisbon extended the EU
exclusive competence much beyond the international trade of goods fully including
international trade in services and trade -related issues such as intel lectual property
and investment. 133 In particular, the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
includes a general part on EU external relations that provides a list of objectives that
the EU should pursue in its relationship with third countries and through its action in
international organisations. Article 21 provides several objectives closely linked with
the EU international commercial policy. Paragraph (e) of Article 21 provides that the
EU shall “encourage the integration of all countries into th e world economy including
progressive abolition of restrictions on international trade” and paragraph (d) requires
that the EU “foster[s] the sustainable economic, social and environmental
development of developing countries with the primary aim of eradica ting poverty”. 134

## 3. Main findings of the case studies
The thesis included the case study of seven free trade agreements between the EU a nd
countries vulnerable to food shortages. Chapter 6 analysed from the perspective of the
human right to food the trade agreement between the EU and 15 Caribbean countries ,
one of the most comprehensive trade agreements the EU has concluded so far.
Chapter 7 took into account a group of six interim trade agreements between the EU
and countries in Sub -Saharan Africa. From the case studies emerged that all the
clauses on import and export of food (tariffs, safeguards and export restrictions)
reduce the capaci ty of the developing countries involved to react to food shortages.
First, all the agreements in order to respect the prescriptions of Article XXIV GATT
eliminate at least 80% of tariff protection exposing vulnerable countries to increasing
competition fro m the EU and limiting their capacity to intervene at the occurrence of
import surges of food from the EU. The Food and Agriculture Organisation considers
import surges dangerous for the realisation of the right to food because they disrupt
the livelihood o f vulnerable farmers already exposed to hunger. To avoid this issue all
the treaties exclude certain sensitive products from the obligation of eliminating
import tariffs. Notwithstanding these exceptions the large majority of EU food
products will be impor ted in the Caribbean and African countries duty free. The
African agreements include additional limitations on the maximum tariff applicable to
sensitive food products imported from the EU . The new regulation promotes EU food
exports in vulnerable countrie s even when this exposes vulnerable groups to food
insecurity. In other words the policy support s the EU export business even if
increasing imports of food in the developing country affect the realisation of the right
to food. The treaties are also likely to affect public revenues of developing countries
hampering their capacity to organise policies to realise the right to food. Overall , the
analysis of the clauses on tariffs manifested the necessity of revising Article XXIV
GATT to allow differential treat ment when vulnerable countries are involved trade
agreements with the EU. Certain aspects of the regulation of tariffs however show that
the negotiators also pursued the objective of imposing limits on developing countries
beyond what required by WTO law. For instance, this is the case of the inclusion of a
maximum tariff for sensitive products imported in African countries which is much
lower than what is required by WTO law.

## 3. Main findings of the case studies
Second, the assessment of the clauses on import safeguards showed that
during ne gotiations very little effort was made to provide Caribbean and African
countries with an efficient mechanism of protection at the occurrence of import surges
of food from the EU. In particular, the treaties do not include a special safeguard
system like t he one of the WTO Agreement on Agriculture which would have allowed
automatic protection of domestic markets in adverse market conditions. The
safeguards provided are slow to implement, are supervised by a supranational
authority and contain almost no diff erential treatment between the EU and vulnerable
countries. In addition, in the African agreements there is no reference to the
possibility of using safeguards to protect food security. The safeguards contained in
the Caribbean agreement contain a referenc e to food security which, even if important
in terms of interpretation of the treaty, looks rhetorical since it does not make the
safeguards easier to implement. The similarities between the regulation of safeguards
of all the seven treaties taken into acc ount manifest that little efforts were made to
tailor the food safeguards on the specific necessities of each vulnerable country. 188
Finally, the regulation of export restrictions of all the agreements limit s
considerably the capacity of developing countries to use them to intervene on the
quantity of food exported abroad at the occurrence of food shortages . This is
particularly evident in the Caribbean case and in four of the African treaties which
ban export quotas and most of export taxes. It is particular ly regrettable that in these
five treaties the negotiators decided not to reproduce the exception of Article XI.2(a)

shortages. Two of the African agreements maintained the excepti on even if they
include a regulation of export taxes considerably more restrictive of WTO. Moreover,
